content:
#1 Hi,

I'm looking into starting a sort of counterpart to TQFT based on the prequantum geometry of helices. According to my calculations these geometric Lie groupoids might actually make up the SU2 sector of a Yang Mills field. Or maybe this is a brutal near miss, who knows? But if I am right this finally allows for computational approaches to gauge theory based on things like synthetic differential geometry and jet calculus.

Paper is here(www.researchgate.net/publication/395585318_Geometric_Computation_Twin_Helices_and_the_Algebra_of_Flow). It outlines all the needed definitions and research directions for this field.

Looking for feedback first.

This paper includes a large amounts of definitions, and I'm not too keen on dumping them on the wiki without some vetting first, despite the fact that I've been told I'm free to do so. It would seem unwise not to ask first. Fire away please.

Ben
subject: Geometric Computability Theory/Computational Gauge Theory

content:
#2 Hi Ben

Based on earlier discussions on the CT Zulip, I don’t think the nLab is the place to put this. You should read the current literature on approaches to gauge theory that uses things like SDG and modal type theory before claiming “this finally allows”. Seeing as multiple mathematicians talking with you couldn’t extract solid definitions about your “helices”, this really falls outside the scope of the nLab.

content: #3 Hi, SDG and modalities/type theory are outlined at the end of section 4, but my approach simply doesn't entirely gel with current approaches since it outgrows the sort of "guardrails" most modalities put in place. As for the base manifold, it's just a trivial fiber bundle that prevents having to deal with topological obstructions.

content:
#6 Allow me to be blunt and quote from the page:

The nLab is not a place to promote pet theories and “revolutionary ideas”.

I’m sorry, but your article reads to me like a “revolutionary idea” that promises vastly more than what looks like is being actually put in. I can only speak for myself, but I don’t see this content being “dumped” on the nLab as a net positive.

despite the fact that I’ve been told I’m free to do so.

actually, no, I don’t think this is really the case. To quote again from the linked page:

The nLab is not a place where you just plop down notes indiscriminately.

Also, on the home page it says

If you are unsure whether what you would like to contribute is appropriate, please ask at the nForum before making the edit.

Thank you for asking here first, even if you think this is merely a courtesy because you were “told you were free to” “dump” your notes on the nLab. From where I stand, the answer would be: please think about small incremental contributions that fill gaps in the exposition of existing theory, and start small. Learn more material yourself, and, most importantly, do not get an LLM to write content for you to add to the nLab. If you aren’t able to write that material yourself, even with books and papers and the rest of the internet that’s not an AI chat bot available to you, then you have to work back to a place where you can start doing that. People who frequent the nLab do not want to have to referee and almost surely rewrite LLM-generated content added to it.

The above is my honest opinion based on working on and with the nLab for nearly two decades as well as having to put out multiple fires over the years.
